newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss expect fewer mad cow cases in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Swiss expect fewer mad cow cases in 1997.

text.p: Switzerland said on Thursday it expects fewer cases of mad cow disease in 1997, has found no evidence of cow-to-calf infection and sees no need for further preventive measures.

A total of 68 cases of bovine spongiform encephalopathy or "mad cow disease" -- a brain-wasting illness that may be fatal to humans who eat infected meat -- were reported in Switzerland in 1995, the Swiss Federal Office of Veterinary Affairs reported.
Swiss cases fell in 1996 for the first time in six years to a total of 45.
Of the nine cases reported so far in 1997, four involved cows born after the ban on feeds containing meal made from animal remains. The ban went into effect in December 1990.
The 1997 numbers did not alter the outlook for a continued decline in the number of cases, the Office of Veterinary Affairs said.

"According to experience in recent years, most cases of BSE show up in the first months of the year. In January 1997 there were six, and in February 1997 already three cases of BSE were reported," BfV said.
"This number is within expectations," the BfV said.
Of the 239 cases of BSE reported in Switzerland since 1990, 18 involved cows born after the ban.
The office said the cases born after the ban were still being subjected to intense scrutiny.

"There is no sign that calves were infected by cows, in other words, through a maternal transmission," it said, adding that some cows which gave birth to calves infected after the ban are still alive, and none of the cows show signs of any central nervous system disease.
The Swiss office said it was most likely that the cases of animals infected after the feeding ban resulted from them having received contaminated feed.

"It cannot be completely ruled out that cattle were fed, either deliberately or by mistake, inadequately heated hog or poultry feed containing brain and spinal material of cows," the veterinary office said.
